beats.intro: Chapter seven. [[sub]]What an exchange rate is, how the currency market works, and how a weaker currency affects trade.
beats.quote: [[a]]An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. [[q]]Dollars per euro, written U S D slash E U R, is one point two zero. That means one euro costs one dollar twenty. The euro is the base currency. [[inv]]Flip it, and one dollar costs point eight three three euros. [[up]]Now the quote rises to one point two six. [[pct]]The euro has appreciated: it buys five percent more dollars. [[dollar]]But the dollar has depreciated by a smaller number: one dollar now buys point seven nine four euros, down four point seven six percent. The two percentages differ, because each is measured from a different starting point.
beats.cross: [[a]]Sometimes you need a cross rate. [[d]]Say a euro costs one twenty dollars, and a pound costs one fifty dollars. [[x]]Then a pound costs one fifty over one twenty, or one point two five euros. [[rule]]Line the currencies up so the common one cancels.
beats.real: [[a]]Currencies trade at nominal exchange rates. [[r]]The real exchange rate adjusts for price levels: the nominal rate, times the foreign price level, divided by the domestic price level. [[ex]]With a nominal rate of one twenty, foreign prices at one hundred, and domestic prices at one ten, the real rate is about one point oh nine. [[mean]]It measures relative purchasing power. A rise in the real rate means the domestic currency buys relatively less.
beats.market: [[a]]The foreign exchange market is the world's largest market. About five trillion dollars change hands each day. [[trade]]Some of it pays for trade in goods and services. [[cap]]An even larger part moves capital: direct investment, and portfolio investment in stocks and bonds. [[hedge]]Companies and investors use it to hedge currency risk. [[spec]]Others use it to speculate on where rates will go.
beats.fwd: [[a]]The spot rate is for immediate delivery, usually two business days later. [[f]]A forward rate is agreed today, for delivery on a future date. [[pts]]It is quoted as the spot rate, plus forward points. [[prem]]If the forward rate is above spot, the base currency trades at a forward premium. Below spot, a discount. [[int]]The currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount, which stops anyone earning a risk-free gain by borrowing in one currency and investing in the other.
beats.ml: [[a]]Does a weaker currency fix a trade deficit? Depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad, and imports dearer at home. [[vol]]Export volumes rise, and import volumes fall. [[ml]]But imports now cost more per unit. The trade balance improves only if demand is price-sensitive enough: the Marshall-Lerner condition. [[j]]And even then, in the short run contracts are already signed, so the balance first gets worse. Later, volumes adjust, and it improves. That is the J-curve.
beats.abs: [[a]]The absorption approach looks at it from the whole economy. The trade balance equals income minus spending, which is called absorption. [[ex]]Here, income is one hundred, spending is one hundred five, and the trade deficit is five. [[spare]]If there is spare capacity, a weaker currency shifts demand to domestic goods, income rises, and the deficit shrinks. [[full]]At full employment, income cannot rise. Unless spending falls, the extra demand only pushes prices up, and the trade balance returns to where it was. [[lesson]]So depreciation alone is rarely a lasting cure. Lasting change needs more saving, or less spending.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]An exchange rate is the price of the base currency in the price currency; percentage changes are not symmetric. [[w2]]Cross rates come from lining up two quotes; real rates adjust for prices. [[w3]]Spot is immediate, forward carries points, and the higher interest rate currency trades at a discount. [[w4]]A weaker currency helps trade only if demand is elastic or spare capacity exists.
